implementation_notes: EF Core 7 added TPC: call UseTpcMappingStrategy() on the root entity type and every concrete type gets its own table containing columns for all of its properties, inherited ones included, while abstract types get no table. The schema is denormalized on purpose, and EF needs hierarchy-unique keys, so it uses one shared sequence by default (SQL Server) because a plain Identity column cannot work; references to the base type lose their foreign-key constraint. Choose TPC over the default TPH when your code mostly queries a single leaf type and benchmarks show the improvement; stay with TPH when queries span the hierarchy.
pitfalls: Identity columns cannot be used as-is: EF needs keys that are unique across the hierarchy, so SQLite (no sequences, no identity seeds) cannot generate integer keys under TPC - use GUIDs or client-side generation.
The denormalization is real: a base property rename must migrate every table, and a reference to the base type cannot be protected by a foreign-key constraint.
Switching an existing model from TPH to TPC is a schema-and-data migration, not a configuration flag: existing rows must be split into the per-type tables.

variants.name: Dapper with one POCO and one statement per table
variants.idiom_name: POCO per concrete table plus hand-written INSERT/SELECT/UNION ALL
variants.implementation_notes: With Dapper the pattern is explicit SQL: one POCO per concrete type carrying the inherited columns as ordinary properties, one INSERT/SELECT per table, and a UNION ALL statement (or separate queries merged in memory) when a mixed collection is needed. Nothing in the mapper knows about a hierarchy, which is exactly what this mapping wants, but the duplicated columns and the shared key source become your responsibility because Dapper maps rows to objects and never generates keys or constraints. It remains the pragmatic route when the schema is owned by SQL rather than by a model.
pitfalls: Dapper does not generate keys: a per-table identity column makes keys collide across the hierarchy, so supply ids from one source (GUID, sequence or Hi-Lo).
The UNION ALL that reconstructs the hierarchy must pad every other subclass's columns with NULL and keep the types aligned, or the mapping fails at runtime.
